item.title: Luxury living and the ultra-rich - When money is no object | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
Sell a penthouse for 12 million euros? Build a luxury villa with an infinity pool? Just another average working day in the lives of Mira van der Zalm and Jürgen Willen: They design and sell luxury properties.
Discretion is paramount here. "German clients tend to be rather reserved when it comes to luxury, whereas foreign clients like to show off what they have," says Jürgen Willen - and he knows what he's talking about. On almost every continent, the architect and his team design luxury villas and interiors for a clientele seeking something truly unique. From bathtubs to car lifts with washing facilities, if it's on the wish-list and can be done, Willen will make it happen. Mira van der Zalm's client base is equally discerning. The estate agent arranges the sale of houses and flats not advertised on the open market - that takes a special level of service. For example, she calls in Jürgen Willen to an Art Nouveau villa in Wiesbaden to check whether it's possible to install an underground parking lot and a spa - and if it can be done in accordance with listed building regulations.

item.author: Quanta Magazine
item.content:encoded:
Astrophysicist Shep Doeleman explains how capturing the first image of a black hole required a telescope the size of the world, and why the next goal is to create a movie.
“The Joy of Why” is a Quanta Magazine podcast about curiosity and the pursuit of knowledge. The mathematician and author Steven Strogatz and the cosmologist and author Janna Levin take turns interviewing leading researchers about the great scientific and mathematical questions of our time. For more episodes visit Quanta Magazine: https://www.quantamagazine.org/tag/the-joy-of-why/
--------
00:00 Why black holes fascinate us 03:27 Meet Shep Doeleman 06:44 How we knew black holes existed 11:28 Turning Earth into a telescope 19:24 Building the Event Horizon Telescope 26:19 M87 vs. Sagittarius A* 35:06 Revealing the first black hole image 39:10 Why black holes look like rings 42:55 Making movies of black holes 46:25 What black hole movies could reveal 49:28 Testing alternatives to black holes 53:12 The joy of seeing the invisible
---------
Black holes are one of the universe’s most exotic and elusive objects. When nothing, not even light, can escape their powerful gravitational grasp, taking a picture of one seems unimaginable. But an image of a black hole, or more accurately its shadow, could offer insights that theory alone may not provide when testing predictions. So how can it be done?
Harvard astrophysicist Shep Doeleman and a team of 250 researchers achieved this extraordinary feat by linking a group of radio telescopes around the world. This network, called the Event Horizon Telescope, produced the first image of a supermassive black hole in the galaxy M87, around 55 million light-years away, and the first image of the black hole at the heart of our galaxy. In this episode, Doeleman tells co-host Janna Levin how he turned the Earth into a telescope capable of seeing a black hole, the incredible level of science and collaboration that was required to achieve this, how the images have furthered our understanding of these exotic objects, and how movies of black holes may be possible by the early 2030s.

item.title: Creatine, debunked
item.author: Vox
item.content:encoded:
Creatine is everywhere right now. But are the claims around this classic supplement actually based in real science? Or are they just more marketing hype?
For decades, creatine has been sold to fitness buffs, as a way to build more muscle, faster. Now it’s being pitched to almost everyone, with influencers, podcasters and celebrity doctors claiming it can sharpen your mind, lift your mood, offset sleep deprivation, and even reverse the effects of Alzheimer’s disease. And these wellness claims are driving a real surge in profit — US sales topped half a billion dollars in 2025.
So what is creatine actually doing in your body? Will it really help you build muscle, or are those dramatic before-and-after photos telling a different story? And when it comes to your brain, is there real evidence behind the claims about memory, mood, and Alzheimer’s, or is the hype getting ahead of the science?
We dug into the research on creatine, from the muscles to the mind, and spoke with exercise scientist Nick Tiller and associate professor Matthew Taylor, whose team at the University of Kansas studied creatine’s effects on people with Alzheimer’s disease.

item.title: The unicorn - In pursuit of magic | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
For centuries, the unicorn has roamed through cultural history, myths and fairy tales. It's been a symbol of healing, destruction - even queer identity. How has this fantastical creature so captured our imaginations?
Legend has it that ever since ancient times, the unicorn has lived in hiding. If it reveals itself at all, it's only ever for a moment - and only ever from a distance. One of the world's most famous mythical creatures, it's been galloping across our cultural histories for centuries. It appears in works of art, on coats of arms and altars, at fountains, on buildings and everyday objects. It appears in fantasy films, has become a symbol of queer identity and an icon of pop culture.
The myth of the unicorn can be traced back to the second millennium B.C. Only quite late in history did it become clear the creature existed in fact only in our imaginations - and yet our fascination with it has never died.
Over time, it's been attributed with countless meanings. It's been thought of as both healing and destructive, wild and untamable, while still serving as a symbol of purity and innocence. And it has always been associated with a deep longing - after someone caught a glimpse of one, they could supposedly never forget it.
But - has anyone ever really seen a unicorn? Where did the idea of a horse with a horn growing from its forehead first come from? How has an animal that has never existed been able to awaken such powerful, true yearning in us for thousands of years? The hunt for its tracks is on...

ABSTRACT In Helsinki, there is a public playground where children learn how computers work. A six-metre tower you climb into as a data packet and slide out as output. A flowchart hopscotch where you jump through conditional statements. A binary abacus you move with your whole body.
Linda Liukas designed this playground. Some computational ideas translated into physical space beautifully. Others fell apart the moment they had to survive a four-year-old. This is a talk about the distance between an abstraction and a body, and the oldest question in computing: how do you make something complex feel simple, without making it simple?
